To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mutations in HAX 1 cause severe congenital neutropenias (Kostmann disease) by interfering with the mitochondrial membrane potential.
HAX1 is an important regulator of mitochondrial function in neutrophil granulo-cytes.
mutations in the gene HAX1 cause SCN and that HAX1 is involved in regulation of the mitochondria.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular pathways that are affected by HAX1 mutations.
the molecular pathogenesis of HAX1-related SCN and with the elucidation of the function of HAX1.
elucidating the function of HAX1 and to identify new targets for treatment of SCN3.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HAX1 is an important protein for cellular viability.
HAX1 mutations lead to a loss of function of this protein, which in turn leads to a loss of cellular viability.
SCN3 is a disease caused by mutations in the HAX1 gene, and that HAX1 has a central role in neutrophil development and viability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HAX1 functions in the control of cell viability and migration.
the loss-of-function mutation in HAX1 causes SCN by interfering with the mitochondrial membrane integrity and/or the control of apoptosis.
SCN3 is a disease with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HAX1 is an important regulator of cellular homeostasis, and its loss leads to an accumulation of apoptotic cells.
the HAX1 protein has a dual role, acting as a negative regulator of apoptosis and as a positive regulator of neutrophil granule formation and migration.
HAX1 is not a “simple” neutropenia gene.
